bankCapital.title: CET1 ratio, RoTE and cost/income ratio
bankCapital.content:
CET1 ratio is Common Equity Tier 1 capital over risk-weighted assets -- the core regulatory solvency measure. RoTE (return on tangible equity) is net income over average tangible shareholders' equity. Cost/income ratio is operating expenses over net revenue -- lower is better.

For Deutsche Bank: management's 2026-2028 'Global Hausbank' targets are CET1 13.5-14.0%, RoTE >13% by 2028 (up from >10% for 2025), and cost/income ratio <60% by 2028. FY2025 actuals were CET1 14.2%, RoTE 10.3%, CIR 64.4% -- within the capital target and meeting the prior RoTE/CIR targets, which is the credibility basis for the more ambitious 2028 goals.

What to watch:

  • CET1 staying inside the 13.5-14.0% operating range (below it forces capital action, sustainably above 14% triggers extra buybacks)
  • Cost/income ratio trending toward the 60% target, not just investment-bank-quarter noise
  • RoTE versus the cost of equity -- DBK has historically earned below it

bookValuePerShare.title: Book value and tangible book value per share
bookValuePerShare.content:
Book value per share is total shareholders' equity divided by basic shares outstanding. Tangible book value per share deducts goodwill and other intangibles first -- the stricter, more commonly cited bank valuation anchor.

For Deutsche Bank: the stock has traded below tangible book value for most of the past decade, a legacy of the 2016-2019 restructuring and litigation years. TBVPS was EUR32.06 at FY2025 (EUR30.98 at FY2024), and the DCF prices the business off a rolled-forward tangible book anchor of roughly EUR32.22 at mid-2026 -- a re-rating toward or above 1x tangible book is the bull case, not assumed in the base case.

What to watch:

  • TBVPS growth path (management targets steady growth from retained earnings plus buybacks)
  • Price/TBV multiple versus European peers
  • Goodwill and intangibles as a share of book value (DBK's gap to tangible book is modest, unlike banks with large acquired goodwill)

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Deutsche Bank Aktiengesellschaft: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Deutsche Bank Aktiengesellschaft: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Deutsche Bank Aktiengesellschaft: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Deutsche Bank Aktiengesellschaft: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Deutsche Bank Aktiengesellschaft: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Deutsche Bank Aktiengesellschaft: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Deutsche Bank Aktiengesellschaft: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Deutsche Bank Aktiengesellschaft: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Deutsche Bank Aktiengesellschaft: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
